lessons.title: Study Session 1: What a Record Actually Is

blocks.text: Introduction Kagiso Seretse spent an entire Tuesday afternoon at a cooperative office in Gaborone trying to answer a simple question: which of the four documents on the shared drive named Grant Agreement Final, Grant Agreement Final Two, Grant Agreement Final Signed, and Grant Agreement Actual Final was the one an auditor could actually rely on. This session works through what separates a genuine record, evidence of a decision or transaction that should never quietly change, from an ordinary document, and why collapsing that difference is where so much records confusion begins. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Define a record and distinguish it from an ordinary working document. Explain the four stages of the records lifecycle. Identify the properties that make a record trustworthy. Recognise the specific moment a working document becomes a record. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Four Files, One Real Answer Kagiso Seretse manages back-office administration for an agricultural cooperative in Gaborone, and when an external auditor requested the co-op's original grant agreement, he discovered four differently named versions on the shared drive, each edited at some point by someone, none clearly marked as the version actually signed and submitted. No single file was wrong to exist. The problem was that nothing distinguished the one that mattered from the drafts that no longer did. 2.2 What Makes Something a Record The International Organization for Standardization's ISO 15489-1:2016, Information and Documentation, Records Management, Part One, defines records management as the systematic control of the creation, receipt, maintenance, use and disposition of records, and sets out the properties that make a record trustworthy: authenticity, that it is genuinely what it claims to be; reliability, that its content can be depended upon as a full and accurate account; usability, that it can be located, retrieved and understood; and integrity, that it remains complete and unaltered. A working draft has none of these properties fixed yet. A record does, from the moment it is finalised. 2.3 Recognising the Lifecycle in Practice Capture: The Moment a Document Becomes a Record A document becomes a record at a specific, identifiable moment, when a decision is finalised, a transaction completed, or an agreement signed, not gradually as it is edited toward that point; naming that moment clearly is what the four unclear file names in Kagiso's case failed to do. Maintenance: Keeping a Record Trustworthy While It Is Active Once captured, a record needs to be kept unaltered and locatable while it remains in active use, which is a different task from simply storing it somewhere and hoping it stays put. Disposition: A Deliberate Decision, Not a Default Eventually every record reaches a point where it is archived permanently or destroyed according to a schedule, and that decision belongs to a deliberate records process, not to whichever drive happens to run out of space first. 2.4 Key Practices Mark the specific moment a working document becomes a finalised record. Name the authoritative version clearly, rather than relying on file names like final or final two. Keep a record's content unaltered once it has been captured. Treat disposition as a deliberate decision made through a records process, not an afterthought. 2.5 A Worked Example: Kagiso's Version Fix After the audit request, Kagiso rebuilt the co-op's file naming so that the moment a document became a record was unmistakable: the actual signed and submitted grant agreement was moved to a separate records folder, renamed with its execution date, and locked from further editing. Every earlier draft stayed exactly where it was, clearly a draft, no longer competing for attention. The next time an auditor asked for a document, Kagiso found the answer inside a minute. None of the co-op's actual paperwork was any different than before. One version, now clearly marked, simply carried an unmistakable claim to being the record that the others no longer did. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating every saved file as equally authoritative, with no clear marker for which one is the actual record, is the habit that produces exactly the confusion Kagiso spent an afternoon untangling. A record earns that name at a specific point, and until that point is marked clearly, no one downstream can tell a finished record from an abandoned draft. 2.7 One Version, Clearly Marked Kagiso's co-op did not need fewer files. It needed one of them, clearly marked, to actually be the record everyone could trust. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned what separates a genuine record from an ordinary working document, and the four stages a record moves through across its lifecycle. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where the same clarity shapes how you build a filing system other people can actually use.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a document in your own work that has multiple saved versions. Is it clear which one is the authoritative record? 2. Name one moment in your own work where a document should be treated as finalised, and describe how you would mark that clearly. Practical Output: Practical Output A short written plan naming how she will mark the authoritative version of one real document in her own work, and how she will distinguish it from earlier drafts. 7.0 References and Further Reading International Organization for Standardization (2016). ISO 15489-1:2016, Information and documentation, Records management, Part 1: Concepts and principles. Geneva: ISO. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Deuteronomy 6:9, on writing the words on the doorposts of the house, a mark meant to last. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:282, on writing down a debt so that it is clearly recorded.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Building a Filing System People Can Actually Use

blocks.text: Introduction Reading a screen with a magnifier for over a decade taught Yamikani Phiri something her sighted colleagues at a health clinic network in Blantyre never had to learn early, that a filing system which only works because you already remember where everything is will fail the first person who does not. Designing a taxonomy that holds up under real, varied use, not just the habits of whoever built it, is what this session teaches. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why filing decisions at the point of storage matter more than search tools. Design a folder and naming taxonomy suited to how people actually search. Apply consistent naming conventions across a shared filing system. Test a taxonomy with real users before adopting it fully. Recognise when a filing system depends too heavily on one person's memory. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A System That Only Worked for One Person Yamikani Phiri coordinates administration for a network of health clinics in Blantyre, working primarily by screen reader and magnification software due to low vision. For years, the clinic network's shared drive was organised the way its founding administrator remembered it, with folder names and structures that made sense only to someone who had built the system from the very beginning. Any new staff member, and especially Yamikani relying on assistive technology, lost significant time simply locating a client intake form. 2.2 Where Filing Failures Actually Come From In 2007, the researcher William Jones published Keeping Found Things Found, an academic study of personal information management, arguing that most information-finding failures trace back to inconsistent decisions made at the moment a file is first stored, not to weak search tools applied afterward. A file misfiled or inconsistently named at the point of saving stays lost regardless of how sophisticated the search function later becomes, which means the real fix belongs at the point of filing, not at the point of searching. 2.3 Designing a Taxonomy for Real Use Naming Consistently, Not Just Logically A folder structure that makes sense to its designer is not the same as one that makes sense to everyone using it; consistent, predictable naming conventions matter more than any single clever organising idea. Structuring Around How People Search, Not How Files Arrived Organising by the categories someone would actually think to search for, client name, date, document type, rather than by the order files happened to arrive, makes a taxonomy usable by someone who was not present when it was built. Testing With Real Users Before Declaring It Finished Asking a colleague unfamiliar with the system to locate a specific file using only the taxonomy, before rolling it out fully, reveals gaps a designer working alone would never notice. 2.4 Key Practices Fix filing decisions at the point of storage, not just at the point of searching. Use consistent, predictable naming conventions across the entire shared system. Structure folders around categories people would actually search for. Test a new taxonomy with someone unfamiliar with it before adopting it fully. Watch for a filing system that only works because one person remembers where everything is. 2.5 A Worked Example: Yamikani's Taxonomy Redesign Yamikani led a redesign of the clinic network's filing system, replacing folders named after whoever originally created them with a consistent structure organised by clinic site, document type and date. Every file name followed the same predictable pattern, which meant a screen reader could announce exactly what a file was without Yamikani needing to open it first. Before rolling the new structure out network-wide, she asked two newly hired administrators to locate five specific files using only the redesigned taxonomy. Their confusion on two of the five revealed naming gaps she fixed before the full rollout, gaps she would never have noticed working alone. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building a filing system that works well for its designer and assuming it will work equally well for everyone else is the mistake that quietly locks an organisation's records behind one person's memory. A taxonomy is only genuinely finished once someone unfamiliar with it can actually use it. 2.7 Findable Without Yamikani in the Room The real test of Yamikani's new system was never whether she could find a file. It was whether someone else could, on a day she was not there to help. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to design a filing taxonomy around how people actually search, and to test it with real users rather than trusting your own memory of the system. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where the same discipline shapes how you choose and sustain a digital document management system.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Review a shared folder you use at work. Could someone unfamiliar with it locate a specific file using only its structure and names? 2. Design one consistent naming convention you could apply across a folder you currently manage inconsistently. Practical Output: Practical Output A short taxonomy plan for one real folder, naming its structure, its naming convention, and one person she will test it with before adopting it fully. 7.0 References and Further Reading Jones, W. (2007). Keeping Found Things Found: The Study and Practice of Personal Information Management. Amsterdam: Morgan Kaufmann/Elsevier. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 25:2, on the glory of kings being to search out a matter. Qur'an, Surah Ta-Ha 20:25-28, on the request to ease the task and untie the knot from the tongue, so that words may be understood.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Choosing and Sustaining a Digital Document Management System

blocks.text: Introduction A logistics firm in Lubumbashi spent a significant sum on a new digital document management system, and within three months barely a third of the staff were actually using it, filing paperwork the old way out of habit while the expensive new system sat mostly empty. Blaise Mukendi led the second attempt at that rollout, and this session follows what he changed. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why EDMS adoption failure is more often organisational than technical. Build staff buy-in before and during a document system rollout. Apply version control discipline within a shared digital system. Distinguish a system's feature list from its actual fitness for daily use. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 An Expensive System, Barely Used Blaise Mukendi works in operations for a logistics firm in Lubumbashi, and when the company first rolled out a digital document management system to replace years of paper-based shipping records, adoption stalled almost immediately. The system had every feature the company had asked for. What it did not have was staff who felt any part of the decision had included them. 2.2 What Actually Sinks an EDMS Rollout In 2004, the researcher Trevor Groenewald published a case study in the SA Journal of Human Resource Management examining an electronic document management system implementation that struggled despite functioning technically as designed. His finding was that the system's partial failure traced to an absence of staff buy-in during the rollout, not to any shortcoming in the software itself, and that the organisation eventually discontinued the system specifically because that human factor was never addressed. 2.3 Rolling Out a System People Will Actually Use Involving Staff Before the Decision Is Final Asking the people who will actually use a system to weigh in before it is purchased, rather than only training them on it after the decision is made, builds the buy-in a purely technical rollout plan cannot provide on its own. Establishing Version Control From the Start Using the system's check-in and check-out features consistently, so that only one person edits a document at a time and every change is tracked, prevents the exact confusion a shared drive without version control invites. Judging Fitness for Daily Use, Not Just the Feature List A system with an impressive list of features is not automatically one that fits how staff actually work day to day; testing it against real daily tasks before full rollout catches a mismatch a features comparison alone would miss. 2.4 Key Practices Involve the people who will actually use a document system before the purchase decision is final. Use check-in and check-out features consistently to maintain real version control. Test a system against real daily tasks, not just its feature list. Address staff resistance directly rather than assuming training alone will resolve it. 2.5 A Worked Example: Blaise's Second Rollout For the second attempt, Blaise organised sessions with staff from each department to walk through their actual daily paperwork before finalising how the system would be configured. Shipping clerks flagged that the proposed folder structure did not match how they actually processed a shipment, and their feedback reshaped the configuration before launch. Adoption reached nearly full staff use within two months, a sharp contrast to the first rollout's stalled third. The software itself had not changed meaningfully between attempts. What changed was that the people expected to use it had actually helped shape how it worked. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming a document system will succeed purely because it has strong technical features, without building genuine staff buy-in into the rollout itself, is the assumption that sank Blaise's first attempt. A system's software quality and its actual adoption are two separate questions, and answering only the first leaves the second to chance. 2.7 The Software Was Never the Problem Nothing about Lubumbashi's shipping clerks changed between the two rollouts except being asked. That single difference decided whether an expensive system sat empty or actually got used. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned that digital document management system adoption depends more on genuine staff buy-in than on technical features alone. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where the same organisational discipline shapes how you build and maintain a retention schedule.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a tool or system introduced at your own workplace. Were the people expected to use it involved before the decision was final? 2. Name one way you could test a new document system against real daily tasks before it is fully adopted. Practical Output: Practical Output A short rollout plan for a document system change, naming who would be consulted before the decision, and one way its fit for daily use would be tested. 7.0 References and Further Reading Groenewald, T. (2004). Electronic document management: A human resource management case study. SA Journal of Human Resource Management, 2(1), 1 to 9. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 4:9, on two being better than one, since they have a good reward for their toil. Qur'an, Surah Ash-Shura 42:38, on those who conduct their affairs by mutual consultation.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Retention Schedules and Safe Disposal

blocks.text: Introduction Would the shipping company Rehema Juma works for in Zanzibar City have been legally exposed if a routine document purge, run against a retention schedule nobody had reviewed in six years, had gone ahead as scheduled? That question, raised almost by accident, is what this session on retention scheduling and safe disposal builds from. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why retention schedules fail most often through neglect rather than poor initial design. Build a retention schedule that reflects current legal and business requirements. Establish a regular review cadence for an existing retention schedule. Dispose of expired records defensibly and securely. Recognise the risk of both premature destruction and indefinite retention. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Purge Almost Run on an Old Schedule Rehema Juma manages records for a shipping company in Zanzibar City, balancing that role with raising her daughter alone, and one afternoon she was minutes from approving a routine document purge when a colleague mentioned an unrelated tax audit requirement that had changed the year before. Checking the company's retention schedule against that new requirement, Rehema realised the schedule itself had not been reviewed in six years, long enough that it no longer matched the law it was meant to satisfy. 2.2 Why Retention Schedules Actually Fail In 2006, the practitioner Laurie Fischer published Condition Critical in ARMA International's Information Management Journal, arguing that records retention schedules most commonly fail not because they were poorly designed at the outset, but because they are written once and never revisited as new business functions, laws and risks emerge. A schedule accurate the year it was written can become a liability years later if nothing about it changes while everything around it does. 2.3 Building a Schedule That Stays Accurate Anchoring Each Retention Period to a Real Requirement Tying each category of record to a specific legal, regulatory or business justification for how long it is kept, rather than a general estimate, gives the schedule something concrete to be checked against later. Setting a Fixed Review Cadence Scheduling a specific, recurring date to review the retention schedule against any new laws or business changes prevents the exact drift that left Rehema's company's schedule six years out of date. Disposing of Expired Records Defensibly Destroying expired records through a documented, secure method, shredding, certified destruction, or verified digital deletion, and recording that the disposal happened, protects the organisation as much as retaining the record ever did. 2.4 Key Practices Anchor each retention period to a specific legal or business requirement, not a general estimate. Set a fixed, recurring date to review the retention schedule against new requirements. Dispose of expired records through a documented, secure and verifiable method. Watch for both premature destruction and indefinite retention as equally real risks. Involve legal or compliance input when a retention period is genuinely uncertain. 2.5 A Worked Example: Rehema's Review Cadence After catching the near miss, Rehema rebuilt the company's retention schedule, tying each record category to the specific law or business rule that set its retention period, and set a recurring annual review date tied to the company's fiscal year close, when regulatory changes were most likely to have been announced. The near-purged tax documents were retained for the newly required period and then disposed of through a certified shredding service, with the disposal logged. The following year's review caught two further law changes before either created a real problem. Rehema's workload had not shrunk; she still balanced the role around her daughter's school schedule. The schedule itself, though, no longer depended on someone happening to overhear the right conversation at the right moment. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Writing a retention schedule once and treating it as permanently correct, without a fixed cadence to check it against new laws and business changes, is the neglect that nearly cost Rehema's company a real compliance failure. A retention schedule is a living document, not a one-time project to complete and file away. 2.7 A Schedule That Keeps Up It was not luck that caught the outdated schedule before real harm was done. It was one colleague's passing comment landing on a records officer who had just begun asking the right question at the right time. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to build a retention schedule tied to real requirements and to sustain it through a fixed review cadence rather than letting it drift out of date. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where the same protective discipline shapes how you control access to confidential records.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Check whether your own organisation's retention schedule, if one exists, has been reviewed within the past year. 2. Identify one category of record in your own work whose retention period you are not certain is still accurate. Practical Output: Practical Output A retention schedule review plan naming one record category, its current retention basis, and a fixed date for its next review. 7.0 References and Further Reading Fischer, L. (2006). Condition critical: developing records retention schedules. Information Management Journal, 40(1), ARMA International. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 3:1 and 3:6, on a time for every matter, a time to keep and a time to cast away. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hashr 59:18, on considering what one has sent ahead for tomorrow.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Protecting What's on Record

blocks.text: Introduction Every file in the loan officer's shared folder at Hinda Ousmane's microfinance institution in Ndjamena was visible to every other employee, including client records containing income, family situation and collateral details that had nothing to do with most of those employees' actual jobs. Hinda, who resettled in Ndjamena after years of displacement and knows firsthand what it costs when personal information moves into the wrong hands, is the one who finally raised it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain the principle behind role-based access control. Apply the need-to-know principle to a shared records system. Assign access permissions through roles rather than individuals. Recognise the risk of overexposed records in a shared system. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Folder Everyone Could See Hinda Ousmane manages records for a microfinance institution in Ndjamena, and shortly after joining, she noticed that the shared drive gave every employee, from loan officers to the office cleaner's supervisor, identical access to every client file, including sensitive income and collateral details. Having resettled in Ndjamena after years of displacement herself, Hinda understood in a way many colleagues did not what it means for personal information to end up somewhere it should never have reached. 2.2 Controlling Access Through Roles In 1992, the researchers David Ferraiolo and Rick Kuhn presented Role-Based Access Controls at the fifteenth National Computer Security Conference, proposing a model where access is granted through roles rather than assigned individually to each person. Their finding was that because roles within an organisation stay relatively stable even as the specific people filling them change, controlling access through roles rather than individuals sharply reduces the ongoing effort needed to keep permissions accurate as staff join, move between positions, or leave. 2.3 Applying Need-to-Know in Practice Defining Roles Before Assigning Access Identifying the distinct roles that actually exist within an organisation, loan officer, records administrator, branch manager, before deciding what each should be able to see, keeps access decisions grounded in job function rather than convenience. Granting Only What a Role Genuinely Needs Limiting each role's access to the specific records its function actually requires, rather than defaulting to broad access for simplicity, closes off exposure that serves no real operational purpose. Reviewing Access When Roles Change Updating access permissions whenever someone changes position or leaves the organisation, rather than letting old permissions linger, keeps the system accurate over time rather than accurate only on the day it was first set up. 2.4 Key Practices Define the actual roles within your organisation before deciding what each can access. Grant each role only the access its function genuinely requires. Update access permissions whenever someone's role changes or they leave. Treat broad, default access as a risk to be closed, not a convenience to be preserved. 2.5 A Worked Example: Hinda's Access Redesign Hinda mapped every role at the institution against the specific records each genuinely needed: loan officers retained full access to their own assigned clients' files, branch managers gained oversight access across their branch, and records administrators like Hinda herself retained full access needed to maintain the system, while unrelated staff lost access to client financial details entirely. The redesign took several weeks of careful mapping, but once complete, updating access for a new hire or a departing staff member became a matter of assigning or removing a single role rather than adjusting dozens of individual permissions. Client records that had sat exposed to the entire staff were, for the first time, visible only to the people whose actual jobs required it. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Granting broad access to everyone by default, on the assumption that restricting it later is more effort than it is worth, is the choice that leaves an organisation's most sensitive records exposed to people who have no actual need to see them. Access control set up around genuine job function costs more time initially and far less risk indefinitely afterward. 2.7 Access That Matches the Job What Hinda's redesign changed was never how much the institution's staff were trusted. It was whether trust and job function were finally the same thing. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to control access to records through defined roles rather than broad default permissions. This closes the protective core of the course and prepares you for Study Session 6, where that same care turns toward auditing and sustaining an entire records programme over time.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Review who has access to a sensitive file or folder in your own work. Does that access match actual job need? 2. Name one role in your own organisation whose access permissions you would adjust if you could. Practical Output: Practical Output A short access mapping exercise naming three roles in her own workplace and the specific records each genuinely needs to see. 7.0 References and Further Reading Ferraiolo, D.F., & Kuhn, D.R. (1992). Role-based access controls. 15th National Computer Security Conference, 554 to 563. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 11:13, on a trustworthy person keeping a confidence. Qur'an, Surah An-Nisa 4:58, on delivering trusts to those to whom they are due.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Keeping the System Alive

blocks.text: Introduction Between hospital visits for his aging mother and a full course load of records coordination duties at a university department in Bujumbura, Pacifique Nduwimana had exactly enough time most weeks to keep the records programme running, never enough to actually improve it. This final session asks a harder question than any before it: how do you sustain and mature a system when the time to build it never quite arrives? 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what a records management maturity model measures. Conduct an honest audit of a records programme's current state. Identify why records programmes commonly stall at a developmental stage. Build a realistic, sustainable improvement plan around real time constraints. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Enough Time to Maintain, Never to Improve Pacifique Nduwimana coordinates records for an academic department at a university in Bujumbura, a role he manages alongside caring for his aging mother through a difficult period of declining health. For over a year, Pacifique kept the department's records programme functioning day to day, but every improvement he identified, better retention tracking, clearer access rules, stayed on a list he never found the uninterrupted time to actually start. 2.2 Why Records Programmes Stall In 2022, the researchers Nathan Mnjama and Joseph Mphunda published a study in the Journal of the South African Society of Archivists applying the ARMA Information Governance Maturity Model to assess a records management programme at Chancellor College, University of Malawi. Their finding was that the programme sat at a developmental maturity stage, with accountability for records assigned to individuals who did not necessarily hold relevant qualifications, and with retrieval of records made difficult by insufficient storage space and inadequate equipment, a pattern the researchers identified as common rather than unusual among comparable programmes. 2.3 Auditing and Sustaining Without Waiting for Free Time Auditing Honestly Rather Than Ideally Assessing a records programme against its actual current state, including gaps that are uncomfortable to name, rather than against an idealised version of what it should be, is what a maturity audit genuinely requires to be useful. Matching Accountability to Real Capacity Assigning records responsibility to someone with both the qualification and the actual time available for it, rather than to whoever is simply present, addresses the specific gap the Malawi study identified as common. Building Improvement in Small, Sustainable Increments Choosing one small, genuinely achievable improvement at a time, rather than an ambitious overhaul that depends on time that may never actually arrive, keeps a records programme moving forward even under real constraints. 2.4 Key Practices Audit a records programme against its actual current state, not an idealised one. Match records accountability to someone with both the qualification and the real time for it. Choose small, genuinely achievable improvements rather than an overhaul dependent on time you may not have. Revisit the maturity audit periodically rather than treating it as a one-time exercise. 2.5 A Worked Example: Pacifique's Honest Audit Rather than waiting for a stretch of uninterrupted time that never came, Pacifique used one afternoon to honestly score his department's records programme against the maturity model's developmental stage indicators. The audit confirmed what he suspected: accountability rested with him alone, without backup, and retrieval was slowed by boxes stored without any consistent labeling in a cramped storeroom. Instead of an overhaul, Pacifique committed to one achievable step each month, first a labeling pass on the storeroom, then a written backup procedure so the programme did not depend entirely on him. Six months in, the programme had genuinely moved past its starting point, not because Pacifique found more time, but because he had stopped waiting for time he did not actually have. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Waiting for an ideal stretch of free time before beginning any records improvement is the pitfall that keeps many capable records coordinators stuck exactly where Pacifique was for over a year. A maturity audit and a small, sustainable next step can both be completed inside a single constrained afternoon, and often that is the only kind of afternoon a records coordinator actually has. 2.7 Moving Forward in the Time That Exists Pacifique's records programme did not mature because his caregiving responsibilities eased. It matured because he finally stopped measuring progress against the time he wished he had. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to audit a records programme honestly against a maturity model and to sustain its improvement in small, realistic increments rather than waiting for time that may never arrive. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Archives and Long-Term Preservation.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Honestly assess one part of your own records practice against its actual current state, not an idealised one. What gap surprises you most? 2. Name one small, genuinely achievable improvement you could complete this month without needing extra time you do not have. Practical Output: Practical Output A written maturity audit of one real records area, naming its current state honestly, and one small, achievable improvement step planned for the coming month. 7.0 References and Further Reading Mnjama, N., & Mphunda, J. (2022). Application of ARMA information governance maturity model for assessment of records management programme at Chancellor College, University of Malawi. Journal of the South African Society of Archivists, 55, 88 to 109. Qur'an, Surah Al-Inshirah 94:5-6, on ease coming alongside hardship.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Rehema was nearly minutes away from approving a document purge. What stopped her?
options: A system error prevented the purge automatically
A colleague's mention of a changed tax audit requirement led her to check an outdated retention schedule
Her manager cancelled the purge without explanation
The documents had already been destroyed previously
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Retention Schedules and Safe Disposal) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Fischer's 2006 article, why do retention schedules most commonly fail?
options: Because they were poorly designed from the very beginning
Because they are written once and never revisited as new business functions and laws emerge
Because organizations never create them at all
Because they are reviewed too frequently
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Retention Schedules and Safe Disposal) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend anchoring each retention period to?
options: A general estimate with no specific basis
A specific legal, regulatory or business requirement
The preference of whichever staff member is available
The amount of physical storage space available
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Retention Schedules and Safe Disposal) before continuing.

quiz.q: Every employee at Hinda's institution had identical access to all client files. What risk did this create?
options: No real risk, since all staff were equally trustworthy
Sensitive client information was exposed to staff with no genuine need to see it
The system became too slow to use
Clients could not access their own records
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Protecting What's on Record) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Ferraiolo and Kuhn's 1992 model, how is access granted?
options: Individually to each specific person by name
Through roles, which stay relatively stable even as the people filling them change
Randomly, to prevent any predictable pattern
Only to the most senior staff member available
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Protecting What's on Record) before continuing.

quiz.q: What did Ferraiolo and Kuhn's research find about controlling access through roles rather than individuals?
options: It significantly increases the ongoing effort required
It sharply reduces the ongoing effort needed to keep permissions accurate as staff change
It has no measurable effect on administrative effort
It only works for very small organizations
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Protecting What's on Record) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Kagiso found four differently named versions of a grant agreement. What was the actual problem?
options: The co-op had too few copies of the document
Nothing distinguished the authoritative record from the drafts that no longer mattered
The auditor had requested the wrong document entirely
The document had been lost completely
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (What a Record Actually Is) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to ISO 15489-1:2016, what does records management systematically control?
options: Only the physical storage location of paper files
The creation, receipt, maintenance, use and disposition of records
Employee performance reviews
Marketing communications only
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (What a Record Actually Is) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What four properties does ISO 15489 identify as making a record trustworthy?
options: Speed, cost, popularity and length
Authenticity, reliability, usability and integrity
Color coding, font choice, page count and formatting
Age, ownership, size and file type
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (What a Record Actually Is) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: The clinic network's filing system worked well for its founding administrator but poorly for others. What did this reveal?
options: The system had too many folders
The system depended too heavily on one person's memory rather than a usable, consistent structure
The clinic needed more staff overall
Digital filing was inherently unreliable
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Filing System People Can Actually Use) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Jones's 2007 research, where do most information-finding failures actually originate?
options: Weak search tools applied after filing
Inconsistent decisions made at the moment a file is first stored
A lack of available storage space
Poor internet connectivity
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Filing System People Can Actually Use) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend structuring folders around?
options: The order in which files happened to arrive
Categories people would actually think to search for, like client name or document type
Random assignment to prevent bias
The alphabetical order of staff names
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Building a Filing System People Can Actually Use) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Blaise's company's first EDMS rollout achieved only about a third staff adoption. What was the underlying cause?
options: The software lacked necessary features
Staff felt no part of the rollout decision had included them
The company had too few staff to use it
The system was too expensive to maintain

finalQuiz.q: According to Groenewald's 2004 case study, what did the organisation's EDMS failure actually trace back to?
options: An absence of staff buy-in during the rollout, not a shortcoming in the software
A complete technical failure of the system
Insufficient funding for the project
A lack of any documented procedures at all
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Choosing and Sustaining a Digital Document Management System) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What did the organisation in Groenewald's case study eventually do with the underperforming system?
options: Continued using it without any changes
Discontinued it, specifically because the human factor was never addressed
Immediately replaced it with an identical system
Sold it to a different organisation
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Choosing and Sustaining a Digital Document Management System) before continuing.
